title: Some thoughts on South Carolina’s surprisingly close Senate race
contentHtml:
If you’re fully exploring the probabilistic landscape in an uncertain electoral environment, you’re inevitably going to end up with some posts that “didn’t age well.” For example, if Democrats have a good night next Tuesday and Peggy Flanagan easily wins in Minnesota, our newsletter from earlier this month that seriously contemplated Michele Tafoya’s chances might be one of those.

If Democrats have a disappointing night, conversely, this post about the South Carolina Senate race will be a candidate for the “didn’t age well” bucket.

But we haven’t examined South Carolina all that seriously. Nor have we given sufficient attention to a possibility that could give Democrats a winning hand in the Senate, even if they fall short in the Palmetto State: disproportionately high turnout among Black voters.

Minnesota and South Carolina, indeed, were two of the three states that The New York Times and Siena University polled in their latest round of surveys, published early this morning.

The third state, Florida, produced the least interesting result, with Republican Ashley Moody ahead by 6 points, pretty much spot-on to FLIPR’s polling average there. The Minnesota and South Carolina surveys were more surprising, although only one of them is really an outlier relative to other polls.

And that state is actually … Minnesota, where NYT/Siena had Flanagan ahead by 14 points, much greater than her 4.7-point lead in the FLIPR average entering the day.

The new poll may reflect Democrats coming home despite Flanagan’s weaknesses as a candidate.1 Indeed, our “simple fundamentals” calculation in Minnesota, based on the generic ballot among likely voters and its partisan lean score, pegs it at D +13.7. Even so, the poll may be on the optimistic side for Flanagan: “probably too hot for Democrats”, as the Times’s Nate Cohn wrote. (Unlike many other pollsters, the NYT/Siena polls do very little herding, and they’ve never been afraid to publish results that differ from the consensus.)

Still, Minnesota comes up as the tipping-point state 6 percent of the time in our simulations, as much as other states that get more attention. Pushing Minnesota from “slightly weird race that could give Republicans a few backdoor outs” to “state that Flanagan will win unless Democrats are having huge problems elsewhere and are screwed anyway” is potentially worth something.2

Paid subscribers get full access to our Election Night livestream with The Argument, GD Politics, and Slow Boring.

The NYT poll in South Carolina is not an outlier

The Times’s poll in South Carolina drew more attention. It showed the race tied 48-48. (Republican Darline Graham was ahead of Democrat Annie Andrews by less than a full point if you go to the decimal place.)

But this poll is not an outlier relative to the polling average in South Carolina, which had shown Graham up by 1.5 points entering the day. Now the average is at … Graham +1.5, still.

That’s partly because the NYT survey wasn’t the only new poll of South Carolina to enter our database overnight. A new Citadel Poll has Graham, who was appointed to succeed Lindsey Graham after he died in July, leading by 3 points. Although in an interesting twist we’ll return to later, the Citadel had Andrews ahead by 6 points among registered voters.3

In my roundup of Senate races this weekend that compared FLIPR’s forecasts against prediction markets, I didn’t take FLIPR’s side in South Carolina. At the time, we gave Andrews a 27 percent chance there, as compared to 20 percent for prediction markets. This is what I wrote about the state:

Here’s where I feel like we start to get into more speculative territory, even though the difference between FLIPR (27 percent for Annie Andrews) and prediction markets (20 percent) isn’t all that large. I suppose I have a reflexive concern about taking the bull case on Democrats in South Carolina given two factors. First, the much overhyped Jaime Harrison race, where he eventually lost to Lindsey Graham (RIP) by 10 points. And second, the state is relatively inelastic. It has a large Black population, a lot of conservative, evangelical whites, and not many swing voters.

Even according to FLIPR, there’s little chance — 4 percent — that South Carolina will be the tipping-point state. If polls are systematically overestimating Democrats in red states, Andrews’s chances are basically zip even if Darline Graham, Lindsey’s sister, is a weak candidate. If the polls are accurate about red-state performance, Democrats could pick up South Carolina if they’re having a fantastic night, but at that point they’ve probably already won Texas and so forth and have more than enough seats in hand.

Ironically, Andrews’s chances have now improved to 27 percent at Polymarket with the new polling, exactly where FLIPR had it previously. Although FLIPR’s odds for Andrews have also ticked up slightly, to 31 percent.

That might actually seem ungenerous to Andrews given how tight the polling is, but FLIPR Classic and FLIPR Deluxe blend polls with “fundamentals” and, in the case of Deluxe, expert ratings. One point I’ve emphasized in recent interviews is that polls and fundamentals actually aren’t all that out of whack in states like Ohio, Texas and Iowa. For instance, a roughly 11-point swing from 2024, in line with FLIPR’s current popular vote forecast, would bring a state like Ohio, which Trump carried by 11 points in 2024, basically to parity.

But that math doesn’t work in South Carolina, which Trump won by 18 points in 2024. Democrats will need basically everything to go right there: first, a serious outperformance for Andrews based on candidate quality and second, turnout patterns that look much different than South Carolina has experienced in the recent past.

Why did FLIPR’s odds for Andrews improve, however slightly, even if our polling average didn’t change? It’s because of that disparity between polls and fundamentals. In a race with no polling at all, FLIPR has no choice but to go entirely on fundamentals. The more polling there is, and the more reliable FLIPR considers polls to be, the more weight it puts on polls instead — although it never entirely zeroes out fundamentals.

Basically, in possession of more data, FLIPR is a bit more confident now that the polls really do show a close race in South Carolina. Those polls might be wrong, and FLIPR still hedges against them a fair bit, projecting Graham to win by about 3 points. But as Bill Scher points out, today’s poll forms a marked contrast to the final NYT/Siena poll in 2020, which rained on the Jaime Harrison parade by showing Graham up 6 points.

Still, as I said, Democrats really need a parlay in South Carolina. To win a Trump +18 state, they’ll need to max out on every factor: turnout and persuasion.
